To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the incidence and the severity of ciliary defects in patients with respiratory disease can be used as diagnostic criteria in the diagnosis of PCD.

(1) cilia from patients with primary ciliary dyskenesis (PCD) have significantly lower beat frequencies, higher incidence of microtuble and dynein arm defects, and greater disorientation of cilia compared to healthy subjects; (2) the number of outer, but not inner, dynein arms correlates with beat frequency; (3) the presence of ciliary abnormalities in patients with bronchiactasis is not diagnostic of primary ciliary diskenesis; and

We identified two patient groups, patients with primary ciliary dyskenesia (PCD, n = 31) who had significantly lower ciliary beat frequency and significantly higher incidences and severities of peripheral tubule defects, central tubule defects and disorientation of cilia than patients with respiratory tract diseases not due to PCL (n = 20).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the ciliary ultrastructure in healthy subjects and patients with respiratory disease and the use of ciliary ultrastructure and beat frequency to diagnose primary ciliary dyskinensis.
the development of a diagnostic method for primary ciliary dyskenesis (PCD) by quantitative analysis of nasal respiratory ciliary ultrastructure and function.
the diagnosis of primary respiratory tract ciliary dyskinesis (PCD) and the development of criteria to aid in its diagnosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ciliary abnormalities found in patients with bronchiectomy are different than those found in PCD patients.
PCD is a heterogeneous disease, which may be caused by different mutations in genes encoding proteins involved in ciliary assembly and/or motility.
PCD is not only a disease of ciliary motility, but also a disease of cilia structure, and that the ciliary structure and function are closely interrelated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the following: (1) Ciliary beat frequency (and hence ciliary motility) is a quantitative parameter that can be used to diagnose PCD.
we developed a method of analyzing cilia in patients with respiratory disease and that we were able to separate patients with PCD from those without PCD.
we were the first to show the correlation between the ciliary ultrastructural defects and the ciliary beat frequency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use cilia to diagnose PCD.

the diagnosis of PCD can be made with confidence if the ciliary beat frequency is <8 Hz, if the number of outer and inner dynein axoneme arms is <6 and 3, respectively, and if the cilia are disoriented by >30 degrees.
the diagnosis of PCD is not as straightforward as one might think.
